lessons.title: The Two Doors: Equity and Debt in One Picture

children.text: Your cousin is opening a second outlet of her restaurant in Indore and needs ₹5 lakh. You have the money. She offers you a choice: lend it to her at 12% a year, to be repaid over three years, or take 10% ownership of the business instead. Same ₹5 lakh, two completely different deals. Pick the loan and you know exactly what you get back, but you get nothing more if the outlet becomes a hit. Pick the ownership and you might get nothing at all, or several times your money.
That choice is the whole of corporate fundraising in miniature. Every company raising money stands at the same two doors.

body.title: Two ways to put ₹5 lakh into your cousin's restaurant

columns.label: Door 1: You lend the money (debt)
points: You are a lender, not an owner
You get 12% a year plus your ₹5 lakh back
You get paid whether the outlet does well or badly
You get no say in the menu, staff or pricing
If the outlet is a blockbuster, you still get only 12%
If it shuts down, you can claim your money ahead of the owners

columns.label: Door 2: You buy 10% of the business (equity)
points: You get 10% of the profits, if and when they are shared
You get nothing in a year with no profit
You get a say, in proportion to your stake
If the outlet is a blockbuster, your 10% could be worth many times ₹5 lakh
If it shuts down, you are paid last, usually nothing

body.text: Debt is a promise to repay a fixed amount, whatever happens. Equity is a claim on whatever is left over, however large or small that turns out to be.

children.text: The One Picture: Where Every Rupee Comes From
Open any Indian company's
balance sheet

and you will find two halves. One half lists what the company owns: factories, machines, inventory, cash, money customers owe it. The other half answers a single question about every rupee of it: whose money paid for this?

markDefs.definition: A statement of what a company owns and what it owes on a single date. Everything it owns must be funded either by owners or by lenders.

body.caption: Equity is the owners' money. Liabilities are other people's money, and debt is the largest part of it.

children.text: There are only two kinds of funding on the right side. Money from owners, which is equity, and money that must be given back, which is debt and other liabilities. A company cannot own a rupee of assets that nobody funded. This is why "equity or debt" is not an academic question. It is the only question the right side of a balance sheet can answer.

body.title: Where to find equity and debt on a real Indian balance sheet

children.text: Indian companies report under Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013, so the labels are standardised. Open the balance sheet of any listed company on screener.in and look for:
Equity share capital
: the face value of all shares issued, which is usually a small number.
Other equity
or
Reserves and surplus
: retained profits plus securities premium. This is where most of the equity actually sits.
Borrowings
under non-current liabilities: loans and debentures repayable after more than 12 months.
Borrowings
under current liabilities: working capital loans, cash credit and anything repayable within 12 months.

Equity share capital plus other equity is what analysts call shareholders' funds or net worth. Add up both borrowings lines and you have total debt. Those two totals are all you need for the ratio in the next section.
Eight Differences That Matter

body.caption: Equity vs debt, side by side

cells: Founders, angels, VC and PE funds, public shareholders
Banks, NBFCs, debenture and bond investors, venture debt funds
Ownership, voting rights, dividends if declared, gains on exit
Interest at an agreed rate plus repayment of principal
None. A company can skip dividends for years
Yes. Interest and principal are due on fixed dates
Diluted. New shareholders get votes and often board seats
Untouched. Lenders get conditions, not ownership
Dividends are paid out of post-tax profit and are not a business expense
Interest is a deductible business expense, which lowers the tax bill
Often collateral: property, plant, receivables or a personal guarantee
Order of payment if the company fails
Permanent. It never has to be returned
Finite. It has a repayment date

body.text: Read that table as a trade. Debt is cheaper and costs you no ownership, but it comes with a legal obligation to pay whatever the business is going through. Equity is expensive and dilutes you, but it never forces a payment. You are choosing which risk you would rather carry.

children.text: How Much of Each? The Debt-to-Equity Ratio
One ratio summarises a company's funding mix. The
debt-to-equity ratio
divides what the company has borrowed by what its owners have in it.

markDefs.definition: Total borrowings divided by shareholders' funds. A rough measure of how much a company relies on borrowed money.

body.caption: Net worth is equity share capital plus other equity. Above 1 means more borrowed money in the business than owners' money.

body.title: Work out the mix
body.prompt: A listed chemicals company reports shareholders' funds of ₹400 crore and total borrowings of ₹600 crore. What is its debt-to-equity ratio? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ₹600 crore divided by ₹400 crore is 1.5. For every ₹1 the owners have in the business, lenders have put in ₹1.50. Whether that is dangerous depends entirely on how steady the company's cash flows are, which is Chapter 3 and Chapter 4 territory.

body.text: There is no single correct debt-to-equity ratio. A power utility with locked-in tariffs can carry 2 or more comfortably. A software services company with almost no fixed assets usually carries close to none. Compare a company only with others in its own industry.

body.label: screener.in
body.description: Search any listed Indian company, open the Balance Sheet tab and read off Equity Share Capital, Reserves and Borrowings. Work out the debt-to-equity ratio for three companies in three different industries and see how far apart they sit.

children.text: The Same Company, Two Funding Choices
Sunrise Foods is a fictional Nashik-based packaged snacks company. It needs ₹10 crore to build a new production line, and it can fund this in either of two ways.
Plan A, all equity
: raise the full ₹10 crore by issuing shares to an investor.
Plan B, half and half
: raise ₹5 crore of equity and borrow ₹5 crore from a bank at 10% a year.

Assume the new line earns an operating profit of ₹2 crore in a good year and only ₹0.4 crore in a bad year, and that the company pays tax at 25%. Surcharge and cess are ignored to keep the arithmetic clean.

body.caption: Sunrise Foods: the same business, two funding plans (₹ crore)

body.title: Return on equity under each funding plan (%)

children.text: Borrowing half the money lifted
return on equity

from 15.0% to 22.5% in the good year. The rupee profit was smaller, but it was earned on half as much owners' money. In the bad year the same borrowing turned a ₹0.30 crore profit into a ₹0.10 crore loss, because the ₹0.50 crore of interest had to be paid regardless.

markDefs.definition: Profit after tax divided by shareholders' funds, shown as a percentage. What the owners earned on the money they have in the business.

stats.label: Interest due either year
stats.context: Not optional, not linked to profits

body.title: Run Plan B yourself
body.prompt: Under Plan B in the good year, operating profit is ₹2 crore and interest is ₹0.50 crore. At a 25% tax rate, what is the profit after tax, in ₹ crore? Answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Profit before tax is ₹2.00 crore minus ₹0.50 crore, which is ₹1.50 crore. Tax at 25% is ₹0.375 crore, leaving ₹1.125 crore, shown as ₹1.13 crore. Divided by the ₹5 crore of owners' money, that is a return on equity of 22.5%.

body.text: Notice what happened in Plan B's bad year. The company still owed ₹0.50 crore of interest on a ₹0.40 crore operating profit. Debt does not wait for a good quarter, and a lender that is not paid can act against the company. Chapter 3 covers exactly what that means.

children.text: Who Gets Paid First
The order of payment is the single most important difference between the two doors, and it explains almost every other difference. Money flowing out of a company follows a fixed queue.
Employees and suppliers
, for running the business day to day.
Lenders
, who receive interest and principal on the dates promised.
The government
, which taxes what is left after interest.
Shareholders
, who receive dividends only if the board declares them out of what remains.
Equity sits at the bottom of that queue in good times and in bad. That is why equity investors demand a much higher return than lenders: they are carrying the risk that nothing reaches the bottom.

body.title: Mind the queue
body.textWithBlank: Because lenders are paid ___ shareholders, they accept a lower return for taking less risk.
body.explanation: The payment queue sets the price of money. Lenders take less risk because they are paid first, so they charge less. Shareholders are paid last, so they demand much more.

body.title: Which door was used?
body.question: A mid-size Indian pharma company announces that it has issued secured non-convertible debentures worth ₹300 crore, carrying 9.2% interest, redeemable in 2031, backed by a charge on its factory. Which door is this?
options: Equity, because debentures are a type of share
Debt, because there is a fixed return, a repayment date and collateral
Equity, because the money can be used for anything
Neither, because debentures are a government instrument
body.explanation: A fixed interest rate, a redemption date and a charge on assets are the signatures of debt. Debenture holders are lenders to the company, not owners of it. Chapter 3 covers how these are issued in India.

body.title: Who takes the hit?
body.question: Sunrise Foods under Plan B has a terrible year and makes an operating loss. Who feels it first?
options: The bank, because its interest is linked to profits
The shareholders, because profits and any dividend disappear while the interest still has to be paid
The government, because it collects less tax
body.explanation: Interest is a contractual payment, so the bank still expects its ₹0.50 crore. Shareholders absorb the loss first, which is the price of sitting last in the payment queue. The government does collect less tax, but it is not the party bearing the loss.

body.title: Two funding needs, one treasury desk
body.scenario: You have just joined the treasury team of a mid-size Hyderabad engineering firm. Two requests land on your desk in the same week. Request 1: the plant head needs ₹4 crore for three months to buy steel for a confirmed government order that will be paid in full on delivery. Request 2: the CEO wants ₹60 crore to enter an entirely new product line with uncertain demand, where losses are expected for the first three years.
body.prompt: Which request points towards debt and which towards equity, and what is your reasoning in each case?
body.modelAnswer:
Request 1 points clearly to debt, most likely a short-term working capital facility or a cash credit line from the company's bank. The need is short, the amount is modest, the inflow is contracted and predictable, and the firm can service and repay it quickly. Raising equity here would mean permanently giving away ownership to solve a three-month cash timing problem, which is an extremely expensive way to fund steel.

Request 2 points towards equity. The payback is uncertain, the horizon is years, and the project is expected to lose money before it makes any. Fixed interest payments through three loss-making years would come out of the existing business's cash flows and could put the whole company under strain. Equity investors accept that risk in exchange for a share of the upside if the new line works. A lender would either refuse or demand heavy security and tight conditions.

The rule you are applying: match the funding to the certainty and the timing of the cash flows it will produce. Predictable and short favours debt. Uncertain and long favours equity.

body.title: Before you argue for one door or the other, check
steps: How certain are the cash flows this money will generate?
When will the money come back, in months or in years?
Can the business service fixed interest in a bad year, not just a good one?
How much ownership are the existing owners willing to give up?
Does the company already carry more debt than its industry peers?
Does it have assets it can offer as collateral, if a lender asks?

body.label: Cost of the two doors in India, roughly
body.value: Debt around 8% to 12%, equity expectations often 15% and above
body.context: A well-rated Indian corporate borrows from banks in roughly the 8% to 12% range, while equity investors in a growth business typically expect 15% or more a year. Equity feels free because nothing has to be paid on a fixed date, but it is the more expensive of the two doors. Chapter 4 shows why.

cards.definition: Money from owners. No repayment date, no fixed return, paid last, carries ownership and votes.
Money from lenders. Fixed interest, fixed repayment date, paid before shareholders, carries no ownership.
Equity share capital plus other equity or reserves. Also called net worth.
Total borrowings divided by shareholders' funds. Compare only within an industry.
Profit after tax divided by shareholders' funds, as a percentage.
An asset pledged to a lender, which it can sell if the borrower does not repay.
Using borrowed money to magnify returns on the owners' money, and the losses too.
Employees and suppliers, then lenders, then tax, then shareholders.

points: Every rupee of a company's assets is funded either by owners (equity) or by money that must be returned (debt).
Debt brings a fixed obligation but no dilution. Equity brings dilution but no obligation to pay.
Interest is a deductible business expense. Dividends are paid out of post-tax profit.
Borrowing raises return on equity in a good year and deepens the damage in a bad one.
Lenders are paid before shareholders, which is why they accept a lower return.
There is no universally right debt-to-equity ratio. Match the funding to how certain and how soon the cash flows are.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Sunrise Foods and the other unnamed companies are fictional illustrations. The interest rate and return ranges are broad indications, not quotes, and change with market conditions. Tax is shown at a simplified 25%, ignoring surcharge and cess.
